utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, would you mind calling the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-05-86-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vinko Pandurevic and Milorad Trbic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Pandurevic and Mr. Trbic, you may sit down. I would ask the Prosecution to introduce itself and can we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Peter McCloskey and Janet Stewart for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the Defence side, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROHAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colleen Rohan --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROHAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Colleen Rohan appearing for Mr. Milorad Trbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Djordje Sarapa, attorney-at-law, representing Mr. Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Judge Antonetti, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dose understand that his microphone is not working? It is working. You may sit down. Please sit down. THE ACCUSED TRBIC: [Interpretation] I am not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear the translation now? THE ACCUSED TRBIC: [Interpretation] Yes. No. Actually, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear the interpretation now? THE ACCUSED TRBIC: [Interpretation] Nothing. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will ask the technician to come in. Let's check this now. I would like to check whether you are receiving the interpretation in your own language. THE ACCUSED TRBIC: [Interpretation] I can hear you now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. So may I ask you to sit down now, please. We have convened this hearing today. Let me remind you that this is a Status Conference we are holding today. The accused Pandurevic had been transferred to the Tribunal on the 23rd of March, 2005. The initial hearing was held on the 31st of March, 2005, and on the 3rd of May, 2005. The accused Trbic had his initial appearance on the 13th of April, 2005, and a new initial appearance was held on the 11th of May, 2005. Pursuant to Article 65 bis, the Trial Chamber must convene a Status Conference within 120 days with a view to organising the exchange between the parties and making sure that the trial goes forward expeditiously, to also check the status of the case, and enable the accused to raise any relevant issue which he or she may wish to raise, and also enable the Judge to check whether the state of health of the accused is good and whether the detention conditions are also appropriate. This is why we are meeting here today. As far as the current motions are concerned, we have a number of -- two pending motions. We have preliminary motions alleging defects in the form of the indictment. As you know, the Prosecution filed a request with a view to obtaining a joinder because you would like this case to be joined with other cases, so that a trial is able to try several accused at the same time, which would enable us to save on our resources and avoid a number of witnesses coming in to testify several times for different cases. This is why the Prosecution asked and seeked [as interpreted] for a leave of joinder. The President of this Tribunal has designated three Judges to render a decision on this joinder motion. As far as I know and to date the Trial Chamber that has been designated has not rendered its decision yet. I would now like to turn to the Prosecutor. Is this right what I am saying now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's my understanding. We know they're working hard, and we hope that it will be relatively soon, because I think everyone knows the importance of that particular motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as the joinder motions are concerned, I'd like to remind you that in civil-law countries, like is the case in my country, a joinder motion filed by the Prosecution when the Judges are seized with this only takes -- it only takes a few minutes to render a decision on the joinder motion with a view to maintaining a good judicial administration. We want -- it is important, therefore, that the Judges render their decision quickly so that we know where we stand. If the joinder is accepted, in that case a new Trial Chamber needs to be appointed, and the Pre-Trial Judge also needs to be appointed. And if no decision is rendered as regards the joinder of cases, in that case we would have to have several different cases; unless the Prosecution, of course, appeals its decision. And in the meantime, we shall just peacefully wait for this decision to be rendered. Notwithstanding this decision which should be taken shortly, I in the meantime need to check with both parties whether the issue relating to disclosure of evidence material is not a problem. As you know, according to Article 66(A)(ii), the Prosecutor provide the Defence with all the evidence material and copies of all the -- copies of the statements of all witnesses within the time limit prescribed by the Trial Chamber. Copies of the statements of all witnesses who the Prosecutor intends to call to testify at trial. Copies of additional Prosecution witnesses shall be made available to the Defence when a decision is made to call these witnesses. Has all this been done?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the Defence have been provided with, of course, all the supporting material. They've also been provided with all the witnesses, witness statements, from the two previous Srebrenica trials. I mean, I think the Defence has -- is working hard to absorb the material that they have been given. We have not yet provided them with a list of our witnesses for the upcoming trial; that is, we are -- of course want to see the make-up of the upcoming trial, see who the various accused will be, and so we have not provided them with a -- any final list yet because we haven't seen the final make-up of the -- of the trial. We're hoping to get that joinder decision soon, in which case we'll be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let me turn now to the Defence counsels, because I would like to ask them whether they have received all this material and whether they have any comments to make given that the Prosecution is awaiting the joinder decision. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROHAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have had as up-to-date no difficulties that I am aware of not only receiving the materials in support of the indictment but also in our dialogue with the Prosecutor who has been quite open with us in making it clear that any information that we may need we can ask for. Of course, the amount of information we have at this point is voluminous, to say the least. It may be that we have requests that come in the future, but at this moment the disclosure as far as on behalf of Mr. Trbic has been fine.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have not had any problems with disclosure or communication with the OTP. Given the stage of the case, we have a lot of material that we have to work on. We're talking here about the supporting material to the indictment that we received on the 3rd of May after the initial appearance and the guilty [as interpreted] plea, and after that we received some more supporting material on several occasions, on the 15th of June. This was disclosed material. On the 20th of July we received also some part of the disclosed material, and after that we received this motion to amend the indictment and join the indictment. Again we received supporting material with that, and we're working on that material. Your question was also about what we think about the disclosure of the names of the witnesses for the Prosecution. At this moment, it is not certain whether this indictment, as it has been proposed, whether it will be approved by the Trial Chamber. However, I believe that it is absolutely certain that these witnesses and the evidence that is mentioned should be disclosed to the Defence, because the Defence assumes that the number of witnesses will be great and a number of them have not been encompassed in the material that we have received, and in that respect we believe that as Defence teams we should talk to the OTP and try and see whether we could get the list of these witnesses. The problem is whether and when the Trial Chamber will render their decision on the amended indictment. And the supporting material that we received with the indictment is not everything that the OTP has or intends to do in terms of the evidence. This is my only observation. I don't have any other concrete proposals, but I believe that this is something that the Defence teams could discuss with the OTP, and I fully believe that we will find a common ground in that respect, and that will be all for me at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll get back to the question of the preliminary motion a bit later. I will -- I would like to talk about disclosure of exhibits. According to Article 68, all relevant material that may suggest the innocence and mitigate the guilt of the accused of the offences they are charged with -- I would like to ask the Defence persons whether the Prosecution has met with its obligation pursuant to this Rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROHAN
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Trbic again, given the amount of information that we have, the number of -- or the amount of EDS disclosure that exists, I am not in a position to answer this question at this moment. I simply don't know. I know that one -- one potential problem which has been discussed with the Office of the Prosecutor, and there are discussions going on, I think, in the hopes that there will be an open and agreeable relationship here in terms of producing information, but one problem is that there are numerous documents. It takes a tremendous amount of time to go through each to identify what they are, to identify whether they, for example, relate to your client, to someone else, whether they contain exculpatory material or not. And I am hoping that in the course of our discussions Defence counsel as well as the Prosecution, that we can work through some way to streamline getting through those documents. But in terms of exculpatory information, certainly -- I'm simply not in a position to answer that question as yet but certainly that review of the material is going forward as efficiently as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would like to ask Mr. McCloskey to shed some light on Rule 68, because according to what Ms. Rohan has just told me, no distinguish -- no distinction is established between Prosecution material and Defence material. It seems to me that the Prosecution has the obligation when it discloses its documents -- if it happens to be an exculpatory material it has to refer to Rule 68. I'd like to put the question now to the Prosecution. Have you sent all the material to -- have you disclosed all material pursuant to 66 (A)(i), 66(A)(ii) and 68 -- have you sent all of the material to the Defence or have you established a distinction between these different types of material? Because we really don't know what's what.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I know we have provided the Defence with all that material. Rule 68 in particular presents a rather difficult problem for everyone. I am not aware of any specific document that suggests that either defendant are not involved in the crimes they are charged with. However, we have many, many statements from various Bosnian Serb army and civilian officers and personnel that differ from each other, and in that potential differences in witnesses are Rule 68 we are endeavouring to provide the Defence with all relevant Serb witness statements of the key people that are involved so that they can determine from their own view the various inconsistencies and credibility problems that may be lurking within our witnesses, because it's clear no one tells the same story twice. And -- but unless I can get very specific requests regarding issues or witnesses, it's impossible for the Prosecution to sort out at this point what the Defence may be looking for in terms of witness statements and their differing accounts. So we had found it was better for both sides to provide the Defence with a complete record of the relevant witnesses in a format where they could search it by computer and identify the material on their own regarding credibility as credibility issues fit into Rule 68. The same thing with the documents and exhibits. We are endeavouring to provide the Defence with all exhibits that will be used at trial and all collections of documents that may be relevant in a searchable format that will allow them to go through this and identify what they feel is relevant to their defence. If I can get specific, again, requests from the Defence about things they may be looking for or need, we will endeavour to try to find that. But as I say, actually, documents or intercepts that suggest these individuals are not involved or mitigated, I don't -- I don't have much in that particular category, and so we don't -- we don't have anything that we've specifically identified in that category of Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The answer provided by the Prosecution is extremely clear, and in line with Rule 68 the Prosecution is telling us today that they have found no document that would come under this Rule. But I think this raises another issue, and this is why I would like to put question to the Defence. From what I understand and from what the Prosecution has just said, you have been provided with all the documents via the electronic system. Does this mean that you do not have hard-copy documents? Does this mean that you have electronic material and nothing else? I'd like to put the question to both of you, to both Defence counsels. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is correct. We have received all the material, almost all the material in the electronic form, and we have a list of the material that was delivered to us in the form of hard copies, but we're talking about very few things compared to what we have received electronically.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROHAN
utterances.text: Yes, I would concur that is the situation. We have also received some disclosure on DVDs and CDs, which is terribly efficient in my opinion for Defence counsel, but it raises its own problems in having your client be in a position to review the information unless they happen to have a laptop computer in the detention centre or they're out on provisional release. They're pretty well foreclosed from reviewing that aspect of the disclosure, which can be of course extremely important for the Defence in terms of working with your client and developing whatever investigative avenues you're going to go through. So it's not in my opinion, speaking again for myself, it's not a huge problem certainly, but it is a bit of a problem. And unfortunately I can't say that I can offer a solution. I don't like to complain without offering a solution and I'm not really complaining. I'm simply raising it as an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I've understood you correctly, the Defence counsels have received all this material in electronic form but -- with a few hard-copy documents, but the accused have nothing whatsoever because they don't have access to the electronic documents. They don't have a computer, and they don't have a CD player. Is that how things stand today? Which from a personal standpoint does not seem to be quite right, because these are cases where we are dealing with documents that are military documents, that contain stamps and signatures, and it would be only normal for the accused and their attorneys to be able to read these documents, hard-copy documents, which are copies of the originals or which should be provided by the Prosecution. This is my standpoint. I don't know what the position of other Judges are, but if I am seized by the Defence with a request to communicate hard-copy documents, I am very much in favour for the accused and his attorneys to be able to have a hard copy of all these documents. Now, let me turn to the Prosecution. Is this how things stand today? In other words, the accused have no documents whatsoever, and the Defence counsels only have documents in electronic form?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is -- I think basically what counsel said is correct. They have a little of everything with mostly electronic documents. But the -- another party which perhaps is not here is -- it has been my understanding that in the past the Defence should have been provided the means by which to obtain laptops for their clients to have in the gaol so that they could look at CDs and look at DVDs. I believe they're given funds or machines to do this. I know many Defence counsel have worked with the authorities in the ICTY to do that. So Defence -- so the clients can have that material. And much of the material is -- some of the key material, for example, the expert report of Rick Butler, I think, has been provided in CD in some cases which is in B/C/S and is something that the client should clearly be able to read. A very voluminous reports with all the documents supporting it attached inside the report in B/C/S so you can click on it to get to the document. This is -- I can tell you, this is the majority of the Prosecution's case, and that is something the clients should have now. And if they don't it's -- they have the ability to get that material from -- from the ICTY because I know other Defence have that. So we're not involved in that process. We help wherever we can because they should absolutely have -- in this day and age I think they should have laptops, each of them. I don't think they should have to share and I think there's been funds made available for them to have that. Regarding hard copies, I prefer hard copies when reviewing. I think all our eyes can't stare at the computer all day. But the theory for that - and again I hate speaking for the client and Defence counsel - but the theory behind that is for the Defence counsel and client to work together with the material, decide which they should have in hard copy, and Defence counsel to print it out on their own ability to print and then provide that to the -- to the counsel [sic]. In fact, that also ensures some confidentiality between client and counsel so -- as opposed to the Prosecutor doing that same process. That puts us in between the two counsel. So I believe that's the way it's design. Hard copies are something that Defence counsel can print out on their own and are given funds to do it. How that relationship is developed with the people here that initiate each Defence counsel is working on that but I haven't heard of any problems but if there are we can assist we will gladly assist. We have been working well with OLAD, with Defence counsel and everyone on these thorny issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I've understood you correctly, the Prosecution is saying now that it is for the Defence counsels to print out these hard copies on their computer and to hand these documents over to the accused. This is a practical way of finding a solution to an essential issue. In other words, these are the exhibits that have to be -- the supporting material of the indictment can therefore be handed over to the accused. And the Defence counsels receive all these documents in electronic form, and the Defence counsels are then free to print this out and hand it over to the accused. Defence counsels, what is your point of view on this? Mr. Sarapa, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe this is an occasion to us to talk about and seek a solution that will be satisfactory for both sides. A certain number of accused in the Detention Unit do have laptops but there is a technical problem that can be solved easily. The Defence believes that whenever it is disclosed electronically it shouldn't be a problem to send the same material to the accused in the Detention Unit and then they could start working on that material. The specific nature of every case is that it deals with a lot of material and both the counsel and the clients have to cooperate because on many occasions it is the clients that can help their Defence counsel, and it is impossible if the clients do not have that material. It has been enabled to us to do that and to -- to search the electronic materials and to forward some of the materials to our clients. Mr. Pandurevic now has all the material I have at my disposal. However, it takes time. There is a time gap. And also there is the matter of cost, which is not negligible. What I think should be the best solution is for the material to be delivered simultaneously to the Defence counsel as well as to the clients. When you have to take into account the distance between ourselves and our clients is a couple of thousand kilometres and we can spend only a couple of days here with them every month, and whenever we contact our clients our time is limited, it is restricted, and these are all technical reasons that make me say that there shouldn't be a reason for which the OTP should not be able to simultaneously disclose the material to the clients at the same time as it is being disclosed to their Defence counsel. I'm not saying that I have a problem with doing it by myself, but it is a technical problem. It is the problem of time, and I really don't see why it should be done simultaneously. This is one of the issues that I was going to raise anyway, but it has come up within the light of everything that has been said so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROHAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I really -- I join in the remarks that Mr. Sarapa has made. I do -- My information is that we do not have funds to obtain a laptop for our clients and I've learned something new here today if that is the case. I know there are Defence counsels here who are thinking perhaps if they have an older laptop to deliver to their client that that is perhaps that is a solution here. I know it's perfectly acceptable to have the laptop in the detention centre and it is one solution. I was unaware that there was funds available for that, and to my mind that solves at least one aspect of this problem because certainly delivering the CDs is far easier than printing out all the material on them which is quite long. I have with Mr. Trbic provided some material that -- I took that course. I printed it out. The file is huge and weighs a lot and it is cumbersome and I don't know how much room they have in their living quarters to store this kind of thing or keep track of it. It is easier to access, I suppose, than a CD if someone is deciding to look through it. There could be problems with that. But again, I'm looking for a solution here, not to complain or create a problem. And if the funds are available for a laptop I think that takes -- that take us well forward into solving certainly a large aspect of this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So we've made some headway on this particular point, and I would like to ask the Defence counsel to contact the Prosecution and try to come up with a solution to avoid the Defence coming up in future and saying we don't have all the documents and the accused don't know which exhibits are going to be used. So kindly find a solution together. If the accused can where they are at the moment be provided with laptop computers by the registry this is a very good thing, but they should know how to use them, of course. That goes without saying. As regards this particular issue, I think if there is a joinder of the cases it will be for the Judge appointed to the Trial Chamber to settle this issue. I have given you my personal point of view. I have told you that I believe it is right for the accused to have access to this material and, if possible, to have hard-copy documents for those documents which are essential. I would now like to turn to the accused to ask them questions about their state of health and to ask them about their detention conditions and to give them the opportunity to take the floor if they so wish. Let me first turn to Mr. Trbic. Before I give the floor to Mr. Trbic, Defence counsel, you would like to add something, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROHAN
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. There are some health issues with Mr. Trbic that I would like to inform the Court of. I think it may be more appropriate to do this in private session and I would ask if we can do that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Registrar, let's move to -- into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Open session. We're currently in open session. Now, as far as your conditions in detention are concerned, are these conditions good? Do people come and visit you? Are you able to make telephone calls? Do you have any complaints to make? THE ACCUSED TRBIC: [Interpretation] All the conditions are satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would you like to raise any other matter or do you think that we have covered all the ground today? THE ACCUSED TRBIC: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. I will put the same question to Mr. Pandurevic. Please stand up. First a question relating to your state of health. Do you have any problems or is everything fine?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please. THE ACCUSED PANDUREVIC: [Interpretation] I don't have any medical complaints. I don't have any complaints about the conditions in the Detention Unit. The conditions are as good as they can be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Is there any particular question you would like to raise? THE ACCUSED PANDUREVIC: [Interpretation] Only a couple of things. I am very happy about the position that you presented about the disclosure of material. As my counsel has suggested, I hope that the disclosure will be done simultaneously. And also as concerns Article 68, exculpatory material, I hope that the indictment will be reduced, and I believe that the Defence and the OTP will find a solution to get hold of this exculpatory material which in my view exists. And this would be all from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have just raised the last issue I wanted to address, namely that of the indictment. As I told you a few minutes ago, there is a -- a motion has been filed, and I'm currently the Pre-Trial Judge of this Chamber, but we had rather wait for the joinder motion to be settled to allow for the Judge and the Trial Chamber that will be seized to render a decision on this matter. I think it is extremely difficult to render a decision as regards the indictment when there is a likelihood that another Trial Chamber and other Judges will have to render a decision on this matter, and I think it would be better if that Trial Chamber and those Judges render a decision on that point. This is why the motion on the defects in the form of the indictment is currently on standby because we are waiting for the decision to be rendered on the joinder motion. We would like this decision to be rendered quickly so that the form of the indictment -- the question of the form of the indictment can be settled. I'm sure everybody understands this, and this is why we are waiting for this decision to be rendered. This decision, I believe, will be rendered shortly. As I have said a while ago, this is not a decision that should take months on end. The Prosecution has filed its motion with a number of arguments, and both parties have already made their submissions, and the three Judges will be able, therefore, to render their decision accordingly. I believe we have covered most of the ground today. I may be seeing you again in four months' time if I am still the Judge who will be appointed to this Trial Chamber. Otherwise, it will be another Judge who will be dealing with this case. This Status Conference relating to the case Pandurevic and Trbic is now currently finished and we stand adjourned.
